primary_text:
$254 for my first store. About $750 for the second. It took one number I had never bothered to count to explain both of them.

Store one ended at our kitchen table on a Sunday night. My wife was asleep, the laptop was open, and the dashboard said about 600 clicks in three weeks and zero orders. I kept hitting refresh like the zero was a glitch.

Forty-four dollars for the website. Two hundred and ten on ads. I added it up on the back of an envelope, $254, and wrote a zero next to it for the sales.

The next morning I told her the store had been "a test." I didn't mention I'd already picked a name for the second one.

That envelope is still in our kitchen drawer. There are two more numbers on it now, one in blue pen and one in pencil, and the smallest one is the one that changed everything.

Why a store at all? I sell solar on commission. Some months are great. Some months the homeowners just aren't interested, and you feel it at the grocery store. I wanted something steadier that was mine. Just something that didn't depend on a stranger in a driveway saying yes.

Anyway. Let me back up.

Store one sold posture correctors. I found the product the way a lot of people do, from a video of a guy saying it was about to blow up. I built the store over two weekends, turned on a $50 ad set, and waited.

Clicks came in. Sales didn't.

So I did what the forums said. I posted my numbers, still no sales, about 600 clicks, and people answered fast. Your landing page. Your targeting. You need more traffic.

I tried new interests. Same product, more clicks, still no sales.

I installed everything. Reviews, discounts, an email pop-up, trust badges, a cleaner product page. No one had bought anything.

I paid for one of those one-week store challenges. I failed the challenge too.

After three weeks I stopped. The product did not sell, so I had to close the store. That's how I explained it to myself, and that's how I explained it to my brother.

Eleven months later I opened store two anyway and told myself I'd learned my lesson.

Store two sold chess boards. Nicer theme, better photos. After ten days of ads, still no orders. People came. Nobody bought. Nobody even put one in a cart.

At 1am one night I typed "I am growing tired of looking at all the traffic and no sales" into a forum, then deleted it. Nobody was going to tell me anything new.

When you do all that work just to find out people don't even want the thing you're selling, it's extremely discouraging. It makes you want to give up. So I did, faster than the first time. I had to stop or I was going to lose all my money.

It felt like pure loss. Money, time, energy, and honestly hope.

For months after that, if anyone brought up online stores, I'd say "I tried dropshipping" the way people say "I tried running." The videos make it seem like easy money when it's really not, and I had decided I wasn't one of the people it works for. I definitely was not an expert.

Then my wife cleaned out the kitchen drawer, held up the envelope, and asked, "What's this?"

Under the $254, in blue pen, was store two: theme, apps, plan fees, ads. About $750. A little over a thousand dollars total.

Then I counted something I had never counted. How many products had those two stores actually tested? I wrote the answer under the money in pencil.

2.

One product per store. A thousand dollars and the better part of two years, and my stores had tested two products.

I looked up what a normal store converts at. A Shopify analytics company publishes the average, and it's about 1.4 percent. Of every hundred visits, a little over one turns into an order. So I ran my own numbers. About 600 clicks at an average store's rate is around eight orders. That's an average, not a promise. But it isn't zero.

Zero isn't what you get when a store is a little off. Zero is what you get when the people come, look at the one thing on the shelf, and don't want it. My traffic was fine. My trust badges were fine. The product missed, and the store never got a second one.

That's why nothing I tried moved. New interests brought more people to the same product. Reviews and badges polished the shelf around the same product. The challenge put a deadline on the same single guess. Every fix was aimed at the store. Not one of them changed what was on the shelf.

A product-research guide I found that week said it plainly: "Most successful dropshippers test 5 to 10 products before finding one that scales profitably."

Five to ten. I had tested two, in two separate stores, and called myself a failure both times.

I didn't have two failed stores. I had two stores that each got one shot, and one guess misses a lot more often than it hits.

That felt lighter and worse. Lighter because it wasn't me. Worse because I still couldn't do anything with it. I couldn't afford five to ten more rounds of what I'd been doing, one product at a time with ads running until the money ran out. That way had cost me a thousand dollars for two answers.

So the envelope went back in the drawer.

A few weeks later, in a tire shop waiting room, I was doing commission math on the back of that same envelope because it was the only paper in my truck.

The woman in the next chair glanced over. "Two fifty-four and a zero. Rough ratio."

I laughed and told her the whole thing in ninety seconds. She'd bought stock for a small chain of gift shops most of her working life, and she asked one question.

"How many products did you put on the shelf?"

"One," I said. "Per store."

"We never stock one thing and wait," she said. "We put a few new things out in small amounts, watch what moves, and send back what doesn't. Most of it doesn't. You don't close the shop because one item sat. You pull the item."

Then the line I still repeat: "You didn't run two stores. You ran one product twice."

That night I searched for what she described and found a page that said it almost word for word. A company called Readymerce builds the store in your name, then releases products in stages instead of one single drop, each with controlled ad testing on a budget you approve. An early performance review decides what stays. What doesn't sell gets replaced with new products, picked from search demand and competition data.

My first reaction wasn't "finally." It was "here we go." I've been burned many times, and a lot of these companies fake the reviews, so I skipped the testimonials and read the fine print.

What got me was a section called "What Is NOT Included": product costs, platform fees, ad spend, and any income, sales or profitability guarantee. Every guru I'd paid made it seem like easy money. This was the first page that agreed with me that it isn't.

On the call I asked straight out: is it $500 and then it goes up to $5,000? It's $500 for the build, one time. The ad budget for the tests is mine, and I set it. Anything past the build, like how much ongoing help, gets quoted on that call.

The refund is seven days from payment, on the $500 fee only, and it ends when you accept delivery, buy any add-on, or ask for further work. Narrow, but written plainly. And the store and its payouts would be in my name either way.

When it was ready, I logged in and checked the owner field first. My name.

The first products went live in stages, each with a test budget I'd approved before a dollar was spent. I knew the most any test could cost me before it started.

The first product didn't do much. Old me would have closed the store that night. Instead the early review came in writing: which product to keep testing, which to replace, and why, with the replacement already lined up. Someone was still on my store after it went live, reading the numbers I used to stare at alone at midnight.

My wife read it over my shoulder. She's watched me close two stores. "So they're not giving up on it."

No. And neither am I.

The store is still open, in my name. The first stage is tested, the first written review is in my hands, and the team is still on it after launch day. For the first time in three tries, a product that didn't sell didn't mean the store was dead. Sunday nights I don't sit there hitting refresh anymore. And when someone brings up online stores, I don't say "I tried." I say I have one.

It was never really the dollars. It was the number of shots. What I needed was a store in my name that gets more than one: products in stages, each with a small test on a budget I approve, and someone who reviews the results and replaces what doesn't sell.

It starts with the $500 Build. Ad spend, product costs and platform fees are extra, and they say so before you pay. No income promise, and I wouldn't trust one.

I was afraid to ever try again. Eventually I did. If I'd stopped at store two, one product nobody wanted would have been the last word on me. Give the next one what mine never got. A second shot.

P.S. The smallest number on that envelope is in pencil. 2. If I'd counted after store one, I'd have skipped store two.
